analysis.research_question_and_background: Virus exposure history, especially first exposure, is believed to shape vaccine efficacy and infection susceptibility, yet mechanistic links between immune responses and epidemiological outcomes are scarce. Recent co‐circulation of SARS‐CoV‐2 variants XFG and BA.3.2 has revealed a striking enrichment of BA.3.2 cases among children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study performed an observational analysis of children and adults, integrating epidemiological modeling with serological testing to assess variant‐specific antibody responses. The focus was on vaccination history and antibody titers in these participants.
analysis.methods: The study combined epidemiological modeling with serology and monoclonal antibody analysis in children and adults to evaluate the dependence of variant‐specific antibody levels on vaccination history. Antibody neutralization assays quantified the ability of sera to block XFG and BA.3.2 infection.
analysis.main_results: Children exhibited a marked enrichment of BA.3.2 infections compared with other variants, indicating increased susceptibility. Ancestral cross‐reactive site I antibodies neutralized BA.3.2 but not XFG, whereas Omicron‐type‐specific site I/III and III antibodies neutralized XFG but not BA.3.2, revealing a tradeoff in antibody specificity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors explain that prior vaccination history shapes the antibody repertoire, accounting for the birth‐year–related differential susceptibility of children to BA.3.2. They propose that pediatric vaccination strategies should prioritize broad neutralization, providing a mechanistic link between immune history and variant risk.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings indicate that children’s vaccination regimens should aim to elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies, guiding vaccine design and public‐health measures to mitigate BA.3.2 risk. Understanding the relationship between immune history and variant susceptibility also informs surveillance and therapeutic monitoring.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to an abstract with no detailed sample size, control groups, or confounder assessment, making the findings preliminary and of moderate confidence. Further studies with larger, well‐controlled cohorts are needed to confirm the mechanistic links between immune history and variant susceptibility.

analysis.summary_en: The preprint investigates why children appear more susceptible to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variant BA.3.2 than to XFG, despite both circulating simultaneously. By reviewing epidemiological data and performing serological and monoclonal antibody analyses in children and adults, the authors show that BA.3.2 cases are enriched in pediatric populations. They find that ancestral cross‐reactive site I antibodies neutralize BA.3.2 but not XFG, whereas Omicron‐type‐specific site I/III and III antibodies neutralize XFG but not BA.3.2, indicating a trade‐off in antibody specificity. The study links this pattern to vaccination history, suggesting that prior immunization shapes the antibody repertoire and drives differential susceptibility. Consequently, the authors argue that pediatric vaccination programs should focus on inducing broad, cross‐variant neutralizing antibodies to reduce infection risk. These results provide a mechanistic explanation for the birth‐year effect on variant susceptibility and highlight the importance of antibody breadth in future vaccine strategies.

analysis.scope_and_question: This article examines how East Asian COVID-19 scholarship conceptualizes vulnerable groups and communication inequality, and what this regional corpus contributes to comparative health communication and the sociology of epidemics.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Drawing on bibliometric mapping and article-level thematic coding of 184 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 on China, Japan, and South Korea, the study compares East Asia-focused research with global COVID-19 literature.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The findings show that East Asian scholarship tends to define vulnerability through situational system mismatch. Children, students, older adults, women, people with disabilities, chronic disease patients, and low-income groups become vulnerable when crisis governance disrupts the institutions, platforms, family relations, and support systems on which they depend.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Even within East Asia, the literature shows important internal differences. Japanese studies foreground aging and norm pressure, Chinese studies emphasize urban-rural educational inequality and youth vulnerability, and Korean studies appear closer to global research in their attention to digital inequality, gendered isolation, discrimination, and health management.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: It argues that future pandemic preparedness requires inclusive communication systems alongside medical and epidemiological capacity.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores how East Asian scholarship conceptualizes vulnerable groups and communication inequality in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. It analyzes 184 peer-reviewed studies from China, Japan, and South Korea published between 2020 and 2025, comparing them with global literature. The findings highlight that vulnerability is defined through situational system mismatch, particularly affecting children, students, older adults, women, people with disabilities, chronic disease patients, and low-income groups. The article identifies four mechanisms through which communication inequality intensifies vulnerability: institutional and technological exclusion, failures of understanding and judgment, interruptions of support, and governance exposure and stigma amplification. It also notes internal differences among East Asian countries, with Japanese studies focusing on aging and norm pressure, Chinese studies on urban-rural educational inequality and youth vulnerability, and Korean studies aligning more closely with global research on digital inequality, gendered isolation, discrimination, and health management. The review concludes that future pandemic preparedness must include inclusive communication systems in addition to medical and epidemiological capacity.

analysis.research_question_and_background: People with severe mental illness (SMI) experienced higher mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection during pandemic peaks, but it was unclear whether this risk persisted after vaccination roll-out. The study addressed a knowledge gap by examining whether excess mortality in people with SMI changed across pandemic stages defined by vaccination roll-out.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective, whole-country cohort study used linked electronic health records from England covering over 99% of the population registered to primary care. The study population included 13,463,945 people with COVID-19 between January 31, 2020, and June 30, 2023, with data on deaths and vaccination status.
analysis.methods: Cox regression models estimated differences in all-cause and COVID-19 mortality between people with and without SMI, stratified by pandemic stages defined by WHO policy and UK vaccination roll-out. SMI was defined as schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, or other affective and non-affective disorders with psychosis.
analysis.main_results: People with SMI had higher all-cause mortality than those without (adjusted hazard ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.53–1.59). The elevated risk was present in stage 1 (aHR 1.27, 1.22–1.32) and increased in stages 2 (aHR 1.56, 1.51–1.61) and 3 (aHR 1.55, 1.50–1.59). By study end, fewer people with SMI were fully vaccinated (79.4%) compared with those without SMI (87.2%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as showing that excess mortality in people with SMI persisted throughout the pandemic despite vaccination, though vaccination partially attenuated COVID-19 mortality risk (aHR 1.25, 1.17–1.34). The novelty lies in quantifying persistent disparities across pandemic stages using whole-country linked data.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the need for targeted public health and clinical strategies to reduce excess mortality and improve vaccination uptake among people with SMI, particularly given their elevated risk across all pandemic stages.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s reliance on routine health records may introduce misclassification or residual confounding, and generalisability to settings without universal healthcare is uncertain. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and potential unmeasured confounding.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective, whole-country cohort study in England assessed mortality following SARS-CoV-2 infection among 13,463,945 people with COVID-19, including 160,190 with severe mental illness (SMI). Using linked electronic health records and Cox regression, the authors found that people with SMI had persistently higher all-cause mortality than those without SMI across all pandemic stages, with adjusted hazard ratios of 1.27 in stage 1, 1.56 in stage 2, and 1.55 in stage 3. Vaccination partially attenuated COVID-19 mortality risk (aHR 1.25), but by study end, fewer people with SMI were fully vaccinated (79.4%) compared with those without SMI (87.2%). The authors conclude that excess mortality in people with SMI persisted despite vaccination, underscoring the need for targeted public health and clinical strategies to address disparities and improve vaccination coverage.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review evaluates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions on maxillofacial and oral surgery (MFOS) services at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital. The central question is how these restrictions affected the volume and types of surgical procedures and diagnoses during the pandemic period compared to the pre-pandemic period.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a retrospective, record review study comparing MFOS patients managed during the COVID-19 period (26 March to 28 December 2020) with the same pre-COVID period one year earlier. Descriptive statistics and χ2 tests were used to summarize and compare the distribution of diagnoses and treatment procedures, with a P-value of <0.05 considered statistically significant.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The study found a substantial decline in MFOS services during the pandemic, with a 41.88% reduction in patient consultations (from 5032 in 2019 to 2926 in 2020, P<0.0001). General anesthetic procedures also decreased by 39.96% (from 453 to 272 cases, P=0.000448). Trauma-related diagnoses decreased from 249 to 154 cases (P=0.556), but trauma remained the most frequent diagnosis during the pandemic. The largest drop in services was observed in alert levels 4 and 5.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review does not provide detailed information on the specific mechanisms or reasons behind the decline in trauma-related diagnoses, nor does it explore the broader implications of these changes on patient outcomes or healthcare systems. The study focuses on descriptive statistics and does not address potential confounding factors or long-term effects.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings suggest that pandemic restrictions significantly impacted MFOS services, particularly in high alert levels. The review implies that regulating alcohol sales and distribution could help reduce trauma admissions, highlighting the need for targeted public health interventions to mitigate the indirect effects of the pandemic on surgical services.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on maxillofacial and oral surgery (MFOS) services at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital. It compares patient consultations and procedures during the pandemic (March to December 2020) with the same period in 2019. The study found a 41.88% decline in patient consultations and a 39.96% reduction in general anesthetic procedures. Trauma-related diagnoses decreased, but trauma remained the most common diagnosis. The largest drop occurred in alert levels 4 and 5. The review suggests that pandemic restrictions significantly affected MFOS services and highlights the potential role of alcohol regulation in reducing trauma admissions. These findings underscore the need for research and policy interventions to address the indirect effects of the pandemic on surgical care.

analysis.scope_and_question: This study investigated associations between building structure and managers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding indoor air quality in welfare facilities for persons with disabilities, comparing facilities with and without coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cluster outbreaks.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A web-based survey was conducted among managers of 242 welfare facilities for persons with disabilities in the Republic of Korea. Facilities were recruited from a national sampling frame of approximately 3,000 facilities, yielding a response rate of 8.1%. The 80-item questionnaire assessed building characteristics and air quality-related KAP scores. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with cluster outbreaks.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Building structure, particularly complex/multi-use configuration, was associated with COVID-19 cluster outbreaks. Facilities in complex/multi-use buildings had higher odds of outbreaks than those in detached buildings did (adjusted odds ratio, 2.21; 95% confidence interval, 1.25-3.91; p=0.006).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: For managerial factors, facilities with outbreaks tended to have lower attitude scores (p=0.02); however, this association did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni correction (adjusted α=0.0083). No significant differences were observed in knowledge or practice scores.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Managerial KAP scores were not definitively associated with outbreaks under the conservative significance threshold, but the observed trends suggest that institutional support, ventilation guidance, and practical training for facility managers may help strengthen future infection-prevention efforts.

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional survey study in South Korea examined the relationship between building structure and managers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding indoor air quality in welfare facilities for persons with disabilities, focusing on facilities with and without COVID-19 cluster outbreaks. The study included 242 facilities, with 50.8% experiencing outbreaks. Results indicated that complex/multi-use buildings were significantly associated with higher odds of outbreaks compared to detached buildings. However, no significant differences were found in knowledge or practice scores, and the association between attitude scores and outbreaks became non-significant after Bonferroni correction. The study suggests that institutional support, ventilation guidance, and training for facility managers could enhance infection prevention strategies. The findings highlight the importance of building design in mitigating the risk of viral transmission in such settings.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of first-generation monovalent inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in reducing infectivity of infected individuals and blocking onward transmission to close contacts, as their role in transmission prevention remains poorly understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used contact-tracing data from Delta outbreaks in Guangzhou and Yangzhou (May–June 2021 and July–August 2021) and the Omicron outbreak in Guangzhou (April 2022), analyzing 323 primary cases and 53,895 close contacts across various contact settings.
analysis.methods: The researchers applied individual-based Bayesian transmission models to estimate vaccine effectiveness on reducing susceptibility and infectivity, adjusting for tertiary transmission, case importation, and exposure history using detailed contact-tracing data.
analysis.main_results: The study found no evidence for vaccine effectiveness on reducing susceptibility (VES) but significant vaccine effectiveness on reducing infectivity (VEI) against both Delta and Omicron variants, with ≥2 doses associated with 45% and 54% lower infectivity respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that first-generation monovalent inactivated vaccines reduce the infectivity of vaccinated individuals, thereby offering community-level protection against novel variants, which is a critical but understudied aspect of herd immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that these vaccines can suppress community transmission by reducing the contagiousness of infected individuals, which has important implications for public health strategies and vaccine deployment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on contact-tracing data and the potential for unmeasured confounding factors, but the evidence is strong given the large sample size and rigorous statistical modeling.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the effectiveness of first-generation monovalent inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in reducing infectivity and blocking transmission during Delta and Omicron outbreaks in China. Using contact-tracing data from Guangzhou and Yangzhou, the researchers applied Bayesian transmission models to estimate vaccine effects on susceptibility and infectivity. They found no evidence of vaccine effectiveness in reducing susceptibility but significant reductions in infectivity for individuals with ≥2 doses, with 45% and 54% lower infectivity for Delta and Omicron variants, respectively. The study highlights the role of these vaccines in reducing community transmission by lowering the contagiousness of infected individuals, which is a critical but understudied component of herd immunity. The findings suggest that these vaccines can contribute to public health strategies by mitigating onward transmission, although the study's reliance on contact-tracing data and potential confounding factors may limit the generalizability of the results.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for rapid, real-time identification of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants during the COVID-19 pandemic, where traditional methods relying on prior lineage classification limit the speed of variant detection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The method was applied to wastewater samples collected from treatment plants serving Swiss catchments in Altenrhein, St. Gallen, Geneva, and Zurich.
analysis.methods: Samples were included only if they had read depths above 40 and genome coverage of at least 90%. Genetic diversity within pooled populations was compared over two time periods to assess changes in viral composition.
analysis.main_results: The approach enabled detection of shifts in genetic populations that corresponded to the emergence of known variants of concern and the Omicron variant with reasonable precision without prior lineage classification.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as demonstrating that their method overcomes the inherently high genomic noise in wastewater compared to clinical samples, providing a novel tool for reliable, real-time variant identification.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This method may inform public health surveillance by enabling timely detection of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants from wastewater, potentially improving resource allocation and outbreak response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is limited to abstract-level data and lacks detailed methodological validation or broader generalizability, warranting cautious interpretation and further study.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a wastewater-based method for identifying SARS-CoV-2 variants in real time without prior lineage classification, addressing the limitation of traditional approaches that rely on predefined lineage signatures. Applied to Swiss wastewater samples from four catchments, the method filtered data based on read depth and genome coverage before comparing genetic diversity over time to detect shifts corresponding to known variants, including Omicron. The authors report that this approach achieved reasonable precision in variant detection despite the high genomic noise inherent to wastewater samples. The findings suggest a valuable tool for public health surveillance, enabling faster and more flexible variant monitoring. However, the evidence is confined to the abstract and lacks detailed validation or broader applicability assessments, indicating a need for further research to confirm reliability and scalability.

analysis.scope_and_question: The study aimed to analyze the sustained concentration of hospital utilization in the capital area among elderly inpatients from non-capital regions in South Korea, both before and during the COVID-19 pandemic, and to identify the characteristics of those who utilized these facilities during the pandemic.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Data were obtained from the Korea National Hospital Discharge In-Depth Injury Survey (KNHDIS) for the periods 2018-2019 (pre-COVID-19) and 2020-2021 (during COVID-19). Statistical analyses, including chi-square tests and logistic regression, were conducted using SAS 9.4 to examine changes in capital-area hospitalization and to identify the characteristics of the study subjects during the pandemic.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The overall rate of capital-area hospitalization among regional elderly patients remained stable at 7.5% both before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Detailed results revealed statistically significant shifts across specific age groups and main diagnoses, with increases observed in some characteristics.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study does not report on the specific mechanisms or implications of the observed shifts in hospitalization patterns related to SARS-CoV-2. It also does not address the potential impact of these patterns on the spread of the virus or the effectiveness of regional healthcare systems.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The observed persistent concentration of hospitalizations in the capital area necessitates the urgent implementation of governmental policies aimed at revitalizing regional medical systems. Hospitals located in non-capital areas are urged to strategically invest in facilities and advanced medical devices and develop targeted strategies to attract regional patients, considering the identified characteristics of elderly regional patients who utilize capital-area hospitals.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the concentration of hospital utilization in the capital area among elderly inpatients from non-capital regions in South Korea before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. It finds that the overall rate of capital-area hospitalization remained stable at 7.5% for elderly patients. However, detailed results show statistically significant shifts in hospitalization patterns across specific age groups and diagnoses. The study highlights the need for governmental policies to support regional medical systems and for non-capital hospitals to invest in facilities and develop strategies to attract patients. The findings suggest that the persistent concentration of hospitalizations may have implications for virus dissemination and healthcare resource allocation.

analysis.scope_and_question: The study focuses on severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and its impact on children during the Omicron BA.5 and XBB waves. The central question is to characterize the clinical features and identify risk factors for severe or critical disease in pediatric patients infected with these variants.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The study is a retrospective analysis of clinical data from pediatric inpatients at the Fifth Hospital of Xiamen between December 2022 and December 2025. The methods include categorizing patients into mild, moderate, and severe/critical groups and using multivariable logistic regression to identify independent risk factors for severe disease.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The study found that the XBB period had a lower incidence of severe/critical disease, lower oxygen requirement, shorter hospital stays, and fewer complications compared to the Omicron BA.5 period. All patients improved or achieved clinical recovery.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The study does not provide detailed information on the biological mechanisms underlying the differences in disease severity between the Omicron BA.5 and XBB variants. Additionally, it does not address the potential impact of other SARS-CoV-2 variants or the long-term effects of post-COVID conditions in children.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms behind the observed differences in disease severity between the Omicron BA.5 and XBB variants. Surveillance and monitoring of pediatric patients during future waves of SARS-CoV-2 infection should prioritize tracking clinical outcomes and risk factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infections in children during the Omicron BA.5 and XBB waves, focusing on clinical characteristics and risk factors for severe disease. The analysis is based on retrospective clinical data from pediatric inpatients at the Fifth Hospital of Xiamen between December 2022 and December 2025. The findings indicate that the XBB period was associated with lower rates of severe/critical disease, reduced oxygen requirements, shorter hospital stays, and fewer complications compared to the Omicron BA.5 period. All patients achieved clinical recovery. The study highlights the need for further research into the biological mechanisms driving these differences and emphasizes the importance of continued surveillance and monitoring of pediatric SARS-CoV-2 infections.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate whether early combination therapy is associated with a lower risk of respiratory failure in severely immunocompromised hosts with COVID-19, as the optimal treatment strategy remains uncertain.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This pragmatic target trial emulation study used observational data collected between 01/01/2022 and 31/03/2024 in 4 tertiary-care hospitals, focusing on immunocompromised patients with mild/moderate COVID-19.
analysis.methods: The study compared monotherapy with antivirals (DAAs) or monoclonal antibodies (MoAbs) to combination therapy of MoAbs plus DAAs using observational data.
analysis.main_results: Of the 303 immunocompromised patients included, 99 (33%) met the primary outcome of respiratory failure, with a lower incidence observed in the combination therapy group (17% vs.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as suggesting that combination therapy may be associated with a reduced risk of respiratory failure in immunocompromised patients with COVID-19, offering a potential treatment strategy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may inform treatment strategies for immunocompromised individuals with COVID-19, particularly in settings where combination therapy is feasible.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on observational data, which may introduce bias and limit causal inference, but the evidence is strong due to the large sample size and clear outcome definitions.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the association between early combination therapy and the risk of respiratory failure in severely immunocompromised hosts with COVID-19. Using observational data from 4 tertiary-care hospitals between 2022 and 2024, the researchers compared monotherapy with antivirals or monoclonal antibodies to combination therapy. The results showed that 33% of patients met the primary outcome of respiratory failure, with a lower incidence in the combination therapy group (17% vs. 42%, p < 0.001). The authors concluded that combination therapy may be preferred over monotherapy in such patients, though the study's observational design limits causal inference. The findings have potential implications for treatment strategies in immunocompromised individuals, particularly during the Omicron-dominant era.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses why SARS-CoV-2 continues to pose a global public health threat despite immune pressure, focusing on the poorly understood role of accessory proteins in transmission beyond the well-characterized Spike protein.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors used the infant mouse model to investigate the contribution of the SARS-CoV-2 accessory protein ORF8 to upper respiratory tract infection, shedding, and transmission.
analysis.methods: Recombinant SARS-CoV-2 strains with and without ORF8 were used to infect mice, and infectious virus shedding from upper respiratory tract tissues and nasal secretions was measured alongside host-to-host transmission efficiency.
analysis.main_results: Mice infected with ORF8-deficient virus (rΔORF8) had less infectious virus recovered from upper respiratory tract tissues and nasal secretions and transmitted less efficiently than mice infected with the isogenic ancestral strain rWA-1 containing intact ORF8.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that ORF8 promotes SARS-CoV-2 transmission by engaging type I interferon-associated inflammatory and secretory programs in the upper respiratory tract that support virus shedding.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study identifies ORF8 as a viral determinant of mucosal immune responses that enhance contagiousness, suggesting potential targets for interventions to reduce SARS-CoV-2 spread.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The use of an infant mouse model and abstract-only evidence limits direct translation to human transmission dynamics, warranting cautious interpretation of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how the SARS-CoV-2 accessory protein ORF8 modulates host immune responses to facilitate transmission. Using an infant mouse model, the authors demonstrate that ORF8 supports efficient upper respiratory tract infection, infectious virus shedding, and host-to-host transmission. Mice infected with ORF8-deficient virus exhibited reduced viral shedding and transmission compared to those infected with ORF8-sufficient virus. Mechanistically, ORF8 engages type I interferon-associated inflammatory and secretory programs in the upper respiratory tract to promote contagiousness. The findings identify ORF8 as a viral determinant of mucosal immune responses that enhance SARS-CoV-2 spread, offering potential targets for interventions.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore how identity-based stigma related to gender affects the mood reactivity of transgender and nonbinary parents to daily family stressors during the COVID-19 pandemic. The research was motivated by the disproportionate impact of the pandemic on transgender and nonbinary individuals due to existing disparities and disruptions in gender-affirming care.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study used a daily diary survey approach, collecting data from 79 transgender and nonbinary parents in the United States between May and June 2020. Participants completed a baseline assessment and an 8-day follow-up survey.
analysis.methods: The study employed multilevel modeling to analyze the association between family stressors and parental negative mood at both between-person and within-person levels. It also examined whether lifetime exposure to gender identity microaggressions moderated mood reactivity to interparental conflicts.
analysis.main_results: Multilevel modeling results showed that both family stressors were associated with parental negative mood at the between-person and within-person levels. Within-person associations were contemporaneous only, with no evidence of prospective next-day effects. Cross-level interactions revealed that lifetime gender identity microaggression exposure attenuated the mood reactivity to interparental conflicts.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that daily family stress processes may serve as intervention targets to support the well-being of transgender and nonbinary parent families during public health crises. This study introduces a novel perspective on how identity-based stigma interacts with family stressors to influence mood.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform targeted interventions to support the mental health of transgender and nonbinary parents during public health emergencies, particularly by addressing the impact of gender identity-related stressors on daily mood.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and a relatively small sample size. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on a single time period and may not be generalizable to all transgender and nonbinary parents.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how identity-based stigma related to gender affects the mood reactivity of transgender and nonbinary parents to daily family stressors during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using daily diary methods, it examines the association between family stressors and parental negative mood at both between-person and within-person levels. Results show that both stressors are linked to negative mood, with no evidence of next-day effects. Lifetime exposure to gender identity microaggressions was found to moderate mood reactivity to interparental conflicts. The findings highlight the importance of addressing gender-related stressors in supporting the mental health of TGNB parents during public health crises. However, the study's reliance on self-reported data and limited sample size may affect the generalizability of the results, suggesting a moderate level of evidence.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review aimed to identify risk factors associated with post-COVID outcomes among patients previously hospitalized for COVID-19. The central question focused on determining which factors are most consistently linked to post-COVID-19 condition, particularly in the context of long-term morbidity following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 principles. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the WHO COVID-19 Global Literature Database were searched for studies published between 1 January 2020 and 24 February 2026. Eligible studies included hospitalized patients with confirmed or probable COVID-19, assessed post-acute outcomes at least 4 weeks after acute infection, hospitalization, recovery, or discharge, and evaluated at least one candidate risk factor. Adjusted effect estimates were prioritized, and random-effects meta-analyses were performed when at least two comparable estimates were available.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Among previously hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, the most consistent risk factors for post-COVID outcomes were female sex, greater acute disease severity or respiratory support, ICU admission, no or incomplete vaccination, and hypertension. These findings were supported by pooled estimates from multiple studies, with female sex showing an odds ratio of 1.94 (95% CI 1.60–2.35) and greater acute disease severity or respiratory support showing an odds ratio of 2.55 (95% CI 1.77–3.68).
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Evidence on risk factors in previously hospitalized populations remains inconsistent due to differences in outcome definitions, follow-up periods, and analytical approaches. The review also noted that additional predictors, including obesity, age, smoking, dysgeusia, symptom burden, and neurological or psychiatric comorbidity, were summarized narratively, indicating a lack of sufficient quantitative data for these factors.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: These findings support risk-based post-discharge follow-up for previously hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection. However, the evidence remains limited by heterogeneous outcome definitions and the small number of studies available for several risk factors. There is a need for further research to standardize outcome definitions and improve the understanding of less well-characterized risk factors.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to identify risk factors for post-COVID-19 condition among previously hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection. The review included 11 studies for qualitative synthesis and seven for quantitative meta-analysis. Key findings indicated that female sex, greater acute disease severity or respiratory support, ICU admission, no or incomplete vaccination, and hypertension were the most consistent risk factors for post-COVID outcomes. The evidence, however, was limited by heterogeneous outcome definitions and the small number of studies for several factors. The review highlights the importance of risk-based post-discharge follow-up and underscores the need for further research to standardize definitions and explore additional risk factors.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed why anosmia and ageusia occur in COVID-19 and what host genetic factors underlie these sensory impairments. It aimed to fill knowledge gaps about the sensorineural mechanisms of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed human genome sequencing data from two cohorts: the University of Iowa (UI) COVID-19 cohort (N = 187) and the National Institute of Health All of Us (AoU) Research Program COVID-19 cohort (N = 947). It employed machine learning methods to classify patients based on genetic variants and genes associated with anosmia and/or ageusia.
analysis.methods: Feature selection techniques were used to construct a variant and gene prioritization pipeline. Models were evaluated using a permutation-based variable importance (PVI) strategy to prioritize candidate variants and genes.
analysis.main_results: The highest held-out test set area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve was 0.735 for the variant analysis and 0.798 for the gene analysis in the UI cohort. For the AoU cohort, the AUROC for the variant analysis was 0.687.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The analysis prioritized several novel and known candidate host genetic factors involved in immune response, neuronal signaling, and calcium signaling, supporting previously proposed hypotheses for anosmia and ageusia in COVID-19.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest potential genetic targets for further research into the mechanisms of sensory impairment in COVID-19, which could inform future diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's AUROC values indicate moderate predictive performance, and the evidence is limited to abstract-level data, which constrains the strength of conclusions about causality or clinical applicability.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the host genetic factors associated with anosmia and ageusia in COVID-19 using genome sequencing data from two cohorts (UI: N=187; AoU: N=947). By applying machine learning and feature selection, the authors developed a pipeline to prioritize genetic variants and genes linked to these sensory impairments. The highest AUROC values were 0.735 (variant analysis, UI) and 0.798 (gene analysis, UI), with 0.687 for the AoU variant analysis, indicating moderate predictive performance. The analysis highlighted candidate genes involved in immune response, neuronal signaling, and calcium signaling, supporting prior hypotheses. While the findings suggest potential genetic targets for further research, the abstract-only evidence and moderate AUROC values limit the strength of conclusions and clinical applicability.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding the comparative pathogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 variants, as genomic evolution has led to immune-evasive strains with unclear impacts on disease severity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A head-to-head comparison of the in vivo pathogenicity of three pivotal strains—ancestral Wild-type (Wuhan lineage), Delta, and Omicron EG.5—was conducted in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, which are highly susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.methods: The study used the K18-hACE2 mouse model to evaluate disease progression, viral burden, and histopathology across the three strains, providing a systematic assessment of their pathogenic potential.
analysis.main_results: All strains progressed to lethality in the mouse model, but they exhibited a distinct gradient in disease kinetics and severity, with the Wild-type strain showing the most rapid progression, highest viral loads, and most severe histopathological damage.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate a clear attenuation in pathogenicity from the ancestral strain through Delta to Omicron EG.5, offering direct experimental evidence of this evolutionary trend.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide crucial insights for risk assessment of emerging variants and highlight the importance of ongoing surveillance to monitor changes in pathogenicity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to an animal model, which may not fully reflect human disease dynamics, but the evidence is strong due to the direct comparison of key variants in a relevant host system.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the comparative systemic pathogenicity and host tropism of ancestral SARS-CoV-2, Delta, and Omicron EG.5 variants in K18-hACE2 mice. The research addresses the need for understanding how viral evolution impacts disease severity, as immune-evasive strains like EG.5 have limited direct pathogenesis data. Using a highly susceptible mouse model, the study systematically compares the in vivo effects of these variants. Results show a gradient in disease progression and severity, with the ancestral strain causing the most rapid and severe outcomes. The Omicron EG.5 variant exhibits significantly reduced pathogenicity, yet retains multi-organ infectivity. These findings offer direct experimental evidence of attenuation in pathogenicity across variants and have implications for risk assessment and surveillance of emerging strains. The study's use of an animal model limits its direct applicability to human disease, but the evidence is robust due to the clear comparative analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the histopathologic and immunothrombotic features of coronary thrombi in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, as mechanisms underlying myocardial infarction after vaccination remain poorly understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective matched cohort study was conducted including 44 matched patients (23 vaccinated and 21 unvaccinated) with STEMI who underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention between January 2021 and March 2023.
analysis.methods: Coronary thrombi obtained by aspiration were analyzed using histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and confocal microscopy for NET detection. Associations between vaccination status and thrombus characteristics were assessed after adjustment for SARS-CoV-2 serologic status.
analysis.main_results: Among 44 matched patients, NETs were identified in 14 vaccinated patients (61%) and 5 unvaccinated patients (24%; P = .01). Vaccination was associated with increased odds of NET-positive thrombi (odds ratio, 5.1; 95% CI, 1.36–19.45; P = .02).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest a potential NET-mediated immunothrombotic mechanism associated with SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, independent of classical vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results may inform future studies on immunothrombotic mechanisms and improve understanding of the relationship between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and cardiovascular complications.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential confounding factors, but the evidence is moderate in strength due to the matched cohort and statistical adjustments.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the immunothrombotic features of coronary thrombi in patients with STEMI following SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. A retrospective matched cohort study was conducted on 44 patients (23 vaccinated and 21 unvaccinated) who underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention between January 2021 and March 2023. Coronary thrombi were analyzed using histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and confocal microscopy for NET detection. Results showed that NETs were more frequently identified in vaccinated patients (61%) compared to unvaccinated patients (24%; P = .01). After adjustment for SARS-CoV-2 serology, vaccination was associated with increased odds of NET-positive thrombi (odds ratio, 5.1; 95% CI, 1.36–19.45; P = .02). The authors suggest a potential NET-mediated immunothrombotic mechanism linked to vaccination, independent of classical immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia. The study's findings may contribute to understanding the relationship between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and cardiovascular complications. However, the retrospective design and potential confounding factors limit the confidence in the results, making the evidence moderate in strength.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether the use of respiratory viral panels (RVP) in children with abnormal urinalysis results increased during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to the prepandemic period, as RVPs are common, expensive tests that often do not alter treatment in such cases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted at a quaternary care children's emergency department, involving children aged 0 to 24 months with abnormal urinalysis results from March 2018 to May 2025. Patients with complex chronic conditions, requiring intensive care or respiratory support, or sepsis were excluded.
analysis.methods: The study used interrupted time series analysis to assess trends in RVP use across the prepandemic, pandemic, and postpandemic periods. The primary outcome was the proportion of children receiving RVP testing, while secondary outcomes included ED revisits, antiviral use, and cost of testing, measured using Medicaid reimbursement fees.
analysis.main_results: The proportion of children receiving RVP testing was 25.0% (95% CI, 23.1-27.0) during the prepandemic period, 68.1% (95% CI, 66.5-69.7) during the pandemic, and 66.1% (95% CI, 64.1-68.0) in the postpandemic period. There was a significant increase during the pandemic compared to the prepandemic period (P < .001), but no change between pandemic and postpandemic (P = .14). Only 134 patients (1.8%) received antivirals, and the total cost of respiratory viral testing was $1 037 978.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that RVP testing increased during the pandemic in children with abnormal urinalysis results and remained elevated postpandemic, highlighting the need for diagnostic stewardship in this context.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the overuse of RVP testing in children with abnormal urinalysis results during the pandemic may have contributed to unnecessary healthcare costs, with limited impact on clinical outcomes such as ED revisits.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its single-center design and retrospective nature, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the lack of randomisation and potential for confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the use of respiratory viral panels (RVP) in children with abnormal urinalysis results. A single-center retrospective cohort study of 7496 children aged 0 to 24 months was conducted from March 2018 to May 2025. The proportion of children receiving RVP testing increased from 25.0% during the prepandemic period to 68.1% during the pandemic, but decreased slightly to 66.1% in the postpandemic period. The study found no differences in ED revisits associated with RVP testing and noted that only 1.8% of patients received antivirals. The total cost of RVP testing was $1,037,978. The authors concluded that RVP testing increased during the pandemic and remained elevated postpandemic, highlighting opportunities for diagnostic stewardship. The study's limitations include its single-center design and retrospective nature, which may affect generalisability, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding the composition and functionality of de novo responses elicited by variant exposures, particularly in the context of rapidly mutating viruses like SARS-CoV-2 where immune memory is dominated by cross-reactive antibodies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved isolating and characterizing hundreds of recall and de novo neutralizing monoclonal antibodies from ancestral-imprinted humans after sequential exposures to SARS-CoV-2 variants, conducted between 2024 and 2025.
analysis.methods: The researchers used sequential exposures to SARS-CoV-2 variants to isolate and characterize neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, focusing on their V(D)J gene usage, neutralization potency, and epitope targeting.
analysis.main_results: De novo variant type-specific antibodies utilized V(D)J genes closer to germline sequences, potently neutralized future variants, and targeted distinct receptor binding domain epitopes compared to ancestral cross-reactive antibodies.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate that de novo antibodies provide distinct neutralizing capabilities against SARS-CoV-2 variants, highlighting the importance of updated booster vaccines in enhancing immune responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform the development of updated booster vaccines that can augment both recall and de novo antibody subsets, contributing to more effective immunity against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-only evidence, and the results are based on monoclonal antibody characterization, which may not fully represent the complexity of natural immune responses. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the immune responses to SARS-CoV-2 variants by isolating and characterizing de novo and recall neutralizing monoclonal antibodies. It reveals that de novo antibodies, elicited by variant exposures, target distinct epitopes and use V(D)J genes closer to germline sequences compared to ancestral cross-reactive antibodies. Despite their potency, neutralizing responses to the 2024-2025 booster were predominantly ancestral cross-reactive, underscoring the need for updated vaccines to enhance both antibody subsets. The findings contribute to understanding the balance between recall and de novo responses and support the use of updated booster vaccines for improved immunity against emerging variants. The study is based on abstract-only evidence, and while the results are informative, the evidence strength is moderate due to the limited scope of monoclonal antibody analysis.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the safety and immunogenicity of OVX033, a nucleocapsid-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate, in healthy adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A Phase 1, first-in-human, randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-escalating study was conducted with 48 participants, previously vaccinated with SARS-CoV-2 licensed vaccines, who received either OVX033 (100μg, 250μg or 500μg; n=12 per cohort) or placebo (n=12, 4 per cohort).
analysis.methods: The study involved immunogenicity assessments, including anti-N IgG and N-specific T-cell responses, and monitored solicited reactogenicity for 7 days, unsolicited adverse events for 28 days, and serious adverse events for 6 months.
analysis.main_results: OVX033 was safe and well-tolerated across all dose levels. Injection site pain was the most common local reaction, while fatigue, headache, and myalgia were the most frequent systemic symptoms.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that OVX033 demonstrated a favorable safety profile and strong boosting of pre-existing N-specific humoral immunity, with no clear dose-effect observed.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that OVX033 could be a viable candidate for enhancing pre-existing immunity against SARS-CoV-2, potentially contributing to broader vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited to a single dose and a small sample size, and the modest T-cell responses observed may require further investigation with a two-dose regimen or adjuvantation.

analysis.summary_en: This Phase 1, first-in-human, randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-escalating study evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of OVX033, a nucleocapsid-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate, in healthy adults previously vaccinated with licensed SARS-CoV-2 vaccines. The study involved 48 participants who received OVX033 at three dose levels (100μg, 250μg, and 500μg) or placebo. OVX033 was found to be safe and well-tolerated, with injection site pain as the most common local reaction and fatigue, headache, and myalgia as the most frequent systemic symptoms. The vaccine elicited a robust anamnestic anti-N IgG response, with titers peaking at Day 29 and 4-fold rises observed in 67-100% of vaccinees. However, N-specific T-cell responses were modest and remained below the limit of quantification. The authors concluded that OVX033 demonstrated a favorable safety profile and strong boosting of pre-existing N-specific humoral immunity, with no clear dose-effect observed. The study's limitations include a single dose and small sample size, and the T-cell response may require further optimization through a two-dose regimen or adjuvantation. These findings provide cautious support for OVX033 as a potential vaccine candidate for enhancing immunity against SARS-CoV-2.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Genomic surveillance has become a cornerstone of epidemic response, yet translating large phylogenies into actionable regional epidemic intelligence remains beyond the reach of most public health systems.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Existing phylogeographic methods are too computationally demanding for routine deployment, creating a bottleneck between genomic data generation and epidemiological insight.
analysis.methods: Here, we introduce STEPHY, a readily deployable graph neural inference toolkit that enables rapid estimation of regional epidemic dynamics directly from large viral phylogenies.
analysis.main_results: We validate STEPHY through simulation studies across complex metapopulation systems, demonstrating accurate recovery of the regional epidemiological quantities and showing that jointly modeling cross-regional dependencies substantially outperforms independent region-by-region analysis.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: By representing phylogenies as region-level graphs and integrating information across connected regional outbreaks, STEPHY jointly estimates region-specific reproduction numbers, recovery rates, source-sink roles, and the most likely index location — epidemiological quantities that directly inform geographically targeted surveillance and intervention.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Inference across phylogenies containing 571 to 7,177 sequences requires only milliseconds, confirming that STEPHY scales to the demands of real-world genomic surveillance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: STEPHY consistently identifies Hovedstaden as the dominant source of viral dissemination, with its source role becoming increasingly pronounced from Alpha through Omicron, revealing a progressive strengthening of spatial transmission heterogeneity across successive variant waves.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces STEPHY, a scalable graph neural inference toolkit designed for rapid estimation of regional epidemic dynamics from large viral phylogenies. The research addresses the challenge of translating genomic data into actionable public health intelligence, which is critical for geographically targeted surveillance and intervention. The study validates STEPHY through simulation studies across complex metapopulation systems, demonstrating its ability to accurately recover regional epidemiological quantities and outperform independent region-by-region analysis. The tool is adaptable to diverse pathogens and surveillance settings, and its performance is confirmed with real-world application to SARS-CoV-2 lineage phylogenies from Denmark. The findings reveal that STEPHY can efficiently process large datasets, making it suitable for routine genomic surveillance. However, the study notes that STEPHY consistently identifies Hovedstaden as the dominant source of viral dissemination, highlighting the importance of spatial transmission heterogeneity across variant waves. The results establish STEPHY as a valuable resource for public health systems aiming to leverage genomic data for epidemic response.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess whether the occurrence, severity, and duration of AE following COVID-19 booster vaccination were associated with subsequent booster uptake during the 2022-2024 autumn booster campaigns in the Netherlands.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We included participants from the Vaccine Study COVID-19 (VASCO), an ongoing prospective cohort study, who were eligible for booster vaccination in 2022-2024. Participants completed a questionnaire on AE one month after booster vaccination.
analysis.methods: Logistic regression was performed to assess the association between the occurrence, severity, and duration of local and systemic AE, and revaccination during the subsequent year. We adjusted for demographics and prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.main_results: In 2022 and 2023, 11,010 and 14,824 participants were vaccinated and completed the AE questionnaire. Of these, 73.7% and 87.0% were revaccinated in subsequent years. The occurrence of systemic AE in 2022 was associated with a lower odds of revaccination in 2023 (OR: 0.84 [95%CI, 0.76-0.93]). The likelihood of revaccination declined with increasing severity - moderate (0.79 [0.66-0.94]) and severe AE (0.45 [0.34-0.60]) - and longer duration (>5 days: 0.72 [0.54-0.95]) of systemic AE. Also, severe local AE (0.38 [0.23-0.60]) and seeking medical care for AE (0.50 [0.34-0.73]) were associated with reduced vaccination uptake. Similar associations were observed for revaccination in 2024.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This study found a lower likelihood of subsequent COVID-19 booster uptake after experiencing systemic AE, particularly when severe or prolonged, or when experiencing a severe local AE.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings underscore the need to address experienced AE in communication strategies, as this may influence the success of vaccination campaigns.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the association between post-vaccination adverse events (AE) and subsequent booster uptake during the 2022-2024 autumn campaigns in the Netherlands. Participants from the Vaccine Study COVID-19 (VASCO) cohort were surveyed one month after booster vaccination. Logistic regression analysis revealed that systemic AE, particularly severe or prolonged ones, and severe local AE were linked to reduced revaccination rates. Additionally, seeking medical care for AE was associated with lower vaccination uptake. Similar patterns were observed in 2024. The findings highlight the importance of addressing AE in public health communication to improve booster campaign success. The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and does not include information on potential confounding factors or limitations in methodology.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate whether the emergence of the SARS-CoV-2 variant XFG was associated with higher rates of sore throat or altered disease severity, as suggested by online news reports and social media.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A participatory surveillance program, Infectieradar, collected weekly reports of respiratory symptoms and disease severity from 39,937 participants in the Netherlands during two specific periods in 2024 and 2025.
analysis.methods: Participants reported SARS-CoV-2 self-test results and a representative subsample with symptoms underwent molecular diagnostic testing and sequencing. Symptom prevalence, burden, and severity were compared between the two periods using adjusted odds ratios and estimated marginal means.
analysis.main_results: Sore throat was not significantly higher during the 2025 wave compared to 2024, and no other symptoms showed significant differences. The number of symptoms and disease severity in the two periods were comparable.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that sore throat is not indicative of the XFG variant and that disease severity during the 2025 wave was not worse than in 2024, based on the comparison of symptomatology and severity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the XFG variant does not cause a notable increase in sore throat or disease severity, which may inform public health surveillance and clinical expectations during future outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on self-reported data and does not include laboratory confirmation for all cases, which may introduce bias. The evidence is moderate due to the reliance on observational data and the potential for unmeasured confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated whether the emergence of the SARS-CoV-2 variant XFG was associated with higher rates of sore throat or altered disease severity. Using data from the participatory surveillance program Infectieradar, the researchers compared symptom prevalence and disease severity between two periods in 2024 and 2025 when the KP.3 and XFG variants were dominant, respectively. They found no significant increase in sore throat or other symptoms during the XFG wave, and disease severity was comparable to the KP.3 period. The authors concluded that XFG does not appear to be linked to increased sore throat or worse disease severity. The study's findings may inform public health surveillance and clinical expectations, but the reliance on self-reported data and lack of comprehensive laboratory confirmation limit the strength of the evidence.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Effects of lockdowns on alcohol use and smoking remain unclear. By exploiting the variation in regional COVID-19 lockdowns in two Chilean regions, we examined their effect on alcohol use and smoking in two university communities.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a quasi-experimental study in university communities in two Chilean regions, Coquimbo and Araucanía. Participants were a longitudinal cohort (n = 896) assessed seven times from July 2020 (t1) to April 2021 (t7).
analysis.methods: Outcomes were weekly grams of alcohol use, heavy episodic drinking (HED) and cigarettes smoked per day.
analysis.main_results: Lockdown between t1 and t3 was associated with an increase of 15.6 g of alcohol used per week (95% confidence interval 1.8; 29.3) and an increase of 0.3 daily cigarettes smoked (95% confidence interval 0.003; 0.5) at t3 (September 2020), compared to the absence of lockdown. When lockdown reversed at t5, we found weak evidence of a reduction in alcohol use and smoking in the region under lockdown. We did not observe changes in HED during the study period.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: COVID-19 lockdown appears to result in an initial relative increase in weekly volume of alcohol use and cigarette smoking compared to a region affected by the COVID-19 pandemic but without lockdown. We did not find evidence of changes in HED.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings suggest that lockdowns may influence alcohol use and smoking behaviors in university communities, which could inform public health strategies for mitigating harmful behaviors during pandemics. The results may help in understanding the behavioral impacts of lockdowns and guide targeted interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report on the limitations of the study design or the strength of the evidence. The study is based on a longitudinal cohort and uses a difference-in-difference analysis, which may have limitations in controlling for confounding variables.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of regional COVID-19 lockdowns on alcohol use and smoking behaviors in two Chilean university communities using a difference-in-difference analysis. A longitudinal cohort of 896 participants was assessed seven times between July 2020 and April 2021. The results indicated an initial increase in alcohol consumption and cigarette smoking during the first lockdown period, with weak evidence of a reduction when lockdowns were reversed. No changes in heavy episodic drinking were observed. The study suggests that lockdowns may influence substance use behaviors, which could inform public health strategies during pandemics. However, the evidence is limited by the study design and the lack of detailed information on limitations.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addressed the public-health concern that SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy may elevate risks for adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, noting that comprehensive neonatal health data following maternal infection remain limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study compared pregnant women with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection to uninfected controls, systematically analyzing maternal complications and neonatal outcomes.
analysis.methods: The authors retrospectively identified SARS-CoV-2-infected and uninfected pregnant women and systematically analyzed maternal complications and neonatal physical indicators and diseases using standard clinical assessments.
analysis.main_results: SARS-CoV-2-infected women had significantly higher complication rates than uninfected controls, and their term and preterm infants showed elevated incidences of myocardial enzyme pattern abnormalities, neonatal pneumonia, central atrial septal defect, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, neonatal clotting diseases, and neonatal respiratory failure.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors concluded that maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection significantly increases preterm birth risk and neonatal morbidity, with first-trimester exposure potentially driving late-pregnancy complications.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support enhanced prenatal surveillance and long-term offspring follow-up to mitigate risks associated with maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The retrospective design and reliance on abstract-only evidence limit causal inference and generalizability, warranting moderate confidence in the reported associations.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective cohort study assessed maternal and neonatal outcomes among pregnant women with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection compared to uninfected controls. Infected women experienced higher complication rates, and their infants showed increased incidences of myocardial enzyme abnormalities, neonatal pneumonia, central atrial septal defect, hyperbilirubinemia, clotting diseases, and respiratory failure. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that maternal SARS-CoV-2 infection elevates preterm birth risk and neonatal morbidity, with potential late-pregnancy complications linked to first-trimester exposure. The study recommends enhanced prenatal surveillance and long-term offspring follow-up. However, the retrospective design and abstract-only evidence constrain causal conclusions and generalizability, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.
